Fifty
fĭf'tŭ
n. and a. (five times ten; the number of release in the Law and of the Spirit's outpouring in the Gospel)
From Anglo-Saxon fiftig — five plus the group-of-ten suffix. Hebrew chamishim is the plural of chamesh, five; the Greek pentekonta gives the New Testament Pentecost, the fiftieth day.

Biblical Definition

Fifty is the number at which things are let go. Seven sabbaths of years are counted and the fiftieth is the jubile, when the trumpet sounds, debts are cancelled, servants go free, and every man returns to his possession (Lev 25:10). Fifty is likewise where the Levite's active service ends — “from thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old” (Num 4:3) — so that the number closes a term as reliably as thirty opens one. It is the second figure in Abraham's intercession, where he begins high: “Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city” (Gen 18:24). And it reappears in the Lord's parable of the two debtors, where five hundred pence and fifty are alike forgiven, and the point is that the smaller debtor loves less because he reckons he owed less (Luk 7:41). Counted forward from the Passover sabbath, the fiftieth day is Pentecost — the release of the Spirit upon the church, the jubile trumpet answered.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fifty as five tens, and notes the scriptural jubilee as the fiftieth year, in which lands reverted and servants were released.

expand to see more

FIFTY, a. Five tens; as fifty men.

FIFTY, n. The number of five tens; 50.

2. Among the Jews, the fiftieth year was the jubilee, in which lands reverted to their former owners and servants were set at liberty.

Note. Pentecost, so called from the Greek, is the fiftieth day from the passover sabbath.

Key Scripture

Gen 18:24 — "Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?"

Num 4:3 — "From thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old, all that enter into the host, to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation."

Luk 7:41 — "There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty."

Exo 30:13 — "This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The jubile is annexed as a proof-text for debt-forgiveness campaigns and land redistribution schemes, cut loose from the covenant and the tribal inheritance that gave it meaning.

expand to see more

Liberation-theology readings and their evangelical imitators lift the fiftieth year out of Leviticus and present it as a divine economic programme for modern states. But the jubile is not a redistribution; it is a restoration. Land in Israel was never alienable in the first place — “the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23) — so what the trumpet did was return each family to an inheritance God had assigned by lot within a tribal covenant that no modern nation possesses. A scheme that takes property from one citizen to give it to another is doing the opposite of what the fiftieth year did.

The principle the fiftieth year does teach is that God sets terms to servitude and debt, that no man's ruin is permanent in a covenant community, and that the church's generosity should have the same flavour of release. Luke 7:41 supplies the spiritual reckoning: the five hundred and the fifty are both forgiven outright, and the danger is not owing much but imagining you owed little.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chamishim (H2572), fifty, plural of chamesh, five; Greek pentekonta (G4004), fifty, and pentekoste (G4005), Pentecost, the fiftieth day.

expand to see more

Hebrew chamishim (H2572) — fifty; the year of jubile (Lev 25:10) and the close of Levitical service (Num 4:3).

Hebrew yobel (H3104) — the ram's horn, and by extension the jubile it announced; the fiftieth year is named for the trumpet that opened it.

Greek pentekonta (G4004) — fifty; the lesser debt of Luk 7:41 and the companies of fifty in Mar 6:40.

Greek pentekoste (G4005) — Pentecost, literally “fiftieth”, counted from the sabbath of the Passover week (Lev 23:15-16).

“Captains of fifty” (Exo 18:21; 2Ki 1:9) — the third rank in Israel's ordering of men.

Usage

"“Until fifty years old” — the number that closes a term of service."

"“Fifty righteous within the city” — the first step of Abraham's descending plea."

"“The other fifty” — the lesser debtor, and the lesser love that follows a small reckoning of sin."
